case.note:
Written by hand, with the three below it, and the labels are arbitrary on purpose. This is the pair MCP001 and MCP013 both flag: `ticket` and `ticket2` take the same subject, body and user, differ only in whether the fourth parameter is called priority or urgency, and are described as "Creates a ticket in the support system with the supplied subject and body." and "Creates a ticket."
No user request can distinguish them, so no correct answer exists and a coin flip is the honest expected result. That is the finding rather than a flaw in the case: the linter says delete one of these, and this is what keeping both costs. The earlier draft scored 8/8 here only because its prompts said "priority high" and "urgency critical" outright, which let the model match a parameter instead of reading a description.

findings.message: Tool names mix conventions: 4 snake_case, 1 camelCase. The odd ones out are `doStuff`.
findings.suggestion: Rename `doStuff` to snake_case so the whole server reads as one API. Mixed conventions make a tool list look assembled rather than designed, and give a model one more axis of variation that carries no meaning.

findings.message: Every word in `search` is generic, so the name says nothing about what the tool operates on.
findings.suggestion: Rename `search` to verb-plus-object form that names the subject -- `search_users`, `create_support_ticket`, `archive_ticket`. A model ranks tools by name before it reads a single description, and a name that would fit on any server in the world gives it nothing to match against.
Write at least one full sentence saying what the tool does and when to use it, then a second saying what it returns. A fragment gives retrieval almost nothing to match a user's phrasing against.

Say something the name cannot: which of several similar tools this is, what it returns, what it costs, when not to use it. A description that repeats the name doubles the weight of the name and adds no new signal.
Describe what `q` is for, what a valid value looks like, and what happens when it is omitted. An auto-generated `title` is not a description -- it is the parameter name with a capital letter.
Describe what `type` is for, what a valid value looks like, and what happens when it is omitted. An auto-generated `title` is not a description -- it is the parameter name with a capital letter.

findings.message: `search.type` is a free-form string, but `type` almost always has a fixed set of valid values.
findings.suggestion: Declare the allowed values as an `enum` on `type` -- in Python, type the argument as `Literal["open", "closed"]` and the schema follows. A model given an open string will invent a plausible value and the call fails at validation, which reads to the user as the tool being broken.

findings.message: Nothing in `search`'s schema shows an example value.
findings.suggestion: Put one concrete value in the description of the least obvious parameter -- "e.g. 'usr_1a2b'" -- or add JSON Schema `examples`. Identifiers and formatted strings are the ones that matter: a model can guess what a search query looks like, and cannot guess what your IDs look like.

findings.message: `search` reads as read-only but declares no `readOnlyHint`.
findings.suggestion: Set `readOnlyHint: true` on `search`. This is the annotation that *earns* you calls rather than costing them: clients use it to run safe tools without interrupting the user, and an unmarked read gets the same confirmation prompt as a delete.

findings.message: `search_users` promises `user` in its name, but the description never mentions it.
findings.suggestion: Say what `user` means here in the first sentence of `search_users`'s description. Retrieval matches a user's phrasing against the description as much as the name, so a description that never names its own subject loses to any sibling whose description does.

findings.message: `search_users` and `search_orgs` share 78% of their meaningful words -- their descriptions are near-identical.
findings.suggestion: Rewrite one of them around what makes it different. If `search_users` and `search_orgs` really do the same thing, delete one; if they do not, the first sentence of each should name the thing only that one handles. Two descriptions this close are a coin flip at selection time, and the model has no way to know it guessed wrong.

findings.message: `search_users` overlaps with `search_orgs`, and its description never says which to prefer.
findings.suggestion: Add a sentence to `search_users` of the form "Use this when X. If you need Y, use `search_orgs` instead." Overlap between sibling tools is normal and usually unavoidable; what separates a server whose tools get picked correctly from one whose tools do not is whether the descriptions say how to choose.
